Under Hungarian ground conditions, what often governs the design of shallow foundations?
The ultimate limit state
The serviceability limit state (settlements)
The groundwater level
The concrete grade of the footing
In many cases it is not the ultimate but the serviceability limit state – settlement and differential settlement – that decides.
What primarily damages the building?
Absolute settlement
Differential settlement
The self-weight of the soil
Thermal expansion
“It is not the absolute settlement but the differential settlement that damages the building” – it causes tilting, sagging, additional internal forces and cracking.
Approximately what relative rotation is very likely to cause an ultimate limit state (failure)?
A relative rotation of 1/150 can already cause failure; 1/500 is generally acceptable structurally.
Which building is more sensitive to differential settlement?
The large, rigid office building
The smaller house with 1–3 storeys and low stiffness
The bridge on piles
All equally
Smaller, lower buildings have lower stiffness – most damaged buildings in Hungary have 1–3 storeys.
Which way do wall cracks rise?
Towards the part with smaller settlement
Towards the part with larger settlement (the part that ends up lower)
Always horizontally
Always vertically
Cracks rise towards the point of larger settlement (towards the part that is lower after the movement) – this helps to find the cause.
Why does reducing the contact pressure not reduce the settlement proportionally?
Because the concrete compresses
Because the wider foundation is heavier, and the stress reaches deeper below it
Because the groundwater rises
Because the influence depth decreases
Two reasons: the wider footing means greater weight, and above all, under the wider foundation the stresses reach greater depths – the influence depth increases.
When is a wider foundation effective?
If there is a softer layer deeper down
If there is a less compressible layer deeper down
Always
Never
It is effective if there are less compressible layers deeper down (case A) – part of the stress is “passed on” to the sand.
Beyond what foundation depth is a strip footing no longer economical?
A strip footing deeper than 2–2.5 m is not economical – then pad footings with ground beams or caisson foundations come into consideration.
What is the twofold effect of a basement?
It insulates and waterproofs
The foundation level may reach a bearing layer, and the weight of the excavated soil increases
It increases the contact pressure and the influence depth
It lowers the groundwater level and the weight
The foundation level reaches (or may reach) a deeper bearing layer, and the weight of the excavated soil increases – this unloads the subsoil.
When does settlement start for a building with two basement levels?
When the first storey is built
When construction reaches the load corresponding to the unloading
Only when the building is occupied
At the moment of excavation
According to the consolidation curve, settlement only started when the load corresponding to the unloading (the weight of the excavated soil) was reached.
Why can soil replacement generally be done only above the water table?
Because the water washes out the cement
Because it cannot be compacted below the water table
Because the geotextile gets wet
Because the pump is too expensive
Below the water table the replacement soil cannot be compacted properly.
